newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC agrees to freeze output; pact to stick with quotas.
newsitem.headline: OPEC agrees to freeze output; pact to stick with quotas.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers agreed Wednesday to freeze their production quotas for six months, sending oil prices sharply higher.

OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman said the producer group agreed to freeze its 25.03 million barrel per day ceiling until the end of the year. He said OPEC members agreed to return to their allocations, but added that no threats were made to overproducers -- led by Venezuela.

Crude oil closed up 49 cents at $19.52 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange and the price surge contributed to a slide in Wall Street stocks on fears that higher oil prices might fuel inflation and push interest rates higher.
Some oil market traders said the statements from the OPEC meeting were ambiguous and that some traders were doubtful that the countries that over-produce would stick to the agreement.
"Who's to say that Venezuela, which has broken its quota in the past, will stick to it," one trader said.
Some traders said they saw a chance of more price falls if OPEC failed to plug some of the leaks in its much-abused quota system.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries is currently pumping some two million barrels per day above its self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million.

"OPEC is going to become important again in the future but they must act now to stop the cheating," said Bob Finch, heading of trading at Vitol SA in London, the world's largest independent oil trader and refiner.
But longer-term, analysts said the market would demand firm proof that nations that have been violating quotas would honour promises given in Vienna to stop the cheating.
"And now the markets will judge," said Libya's Abdullah Salem al-Badri, president of the cartel.
Chronic violations have lifted actual output some two million barrels above the ceiling, and prices have fallen from $25 since January.
Announcing Wednesday's decision, OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman said that all 11 cartel members gave individual pledges that they would adhere to mandatory limits.
Lukman said no threats had been made against alleged violators but that they had made promises to colleagues and OPEC believed them.
Some seasoned OPEC-watchers who were sceptical, among them U.S. oilman Oscar Wyatt, doubted whether demand would be strong enough to lift prices if OPEC produces as much as it is likely to.
"There is nothing to lift this market ... it would have to be some external event other than consumption," said Wyatt, retiring chairman of Coastal Corp.
"People will not believe that anything has changed until they see it," said Leo Drollas, economist at the London-based Centre for Global Energy Studies.
He said that Venezuela, which is above quota by a huge 800,000 barrels daily, "simply cannot deliver on a commitment like that."
Nigeria is another cash-pinched Third World country that monitors say is over-producing.
A strong line on violations by OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia, teamed with Gulf rival Iran, took traders by surprise.

Venezuela's minister, Erwin Arrieta, was earlier summoned to a private session with Saudi Arabia's Ali Naimi and Gholamrezah Aghazadeh of Iran, which a Gulf delegate said was intended to "emphasise the need for quota compliance."
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue-lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said Saudi Arabia was in no mood to threaten to turn up the flow on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
The new OPEC accord is due to be rubber-stamped at a plenary session of the OPEC conference on Thursday.
